t: What Thermal Paste Does Between CPU and Cooler
title: What Thermal Paste Does Between CPU and Cooler
description: Thermal paste (thermal compound, TIM) fills the microscopic gaps between the CPU heatspreader and the cooler base — air is a terrible conductor, and even mirror-flat metal touches only at high spots. The paste's job is displacing air with something more conductive. Too little leaves air gaps; too much insulates. The right amount is a thin, even layer — and that is what application method is all about.

demo.program:
print("Metal touches metal only at high spots; the rest is air (terrible conductor).")
print("Paste displaces air with conductive compound.")
print("Too little: air gaps. Too much: insulates. Right: thin, even layer.")

t: Pea vs Line vs Spread: The Application Methods
title: Pea vs Line vs Spread: The Application Methods
description: The pea method (a pea-sized dot center) lets cooler pressure spread the paste — simplest and most popular. The line method suits rectangular dies. Manual spreading with a card gives the most even layer and full coverage proof, at the cost of technique. Tests show all methods perform within a degree or two when the amount is right — amount matters more than pattern.

demo.program:
print("Pea (dot center): pressure spreads it. Simplest, most popular.")
print("Line: rectangular dies. Spread (card): most even, full-coverage proof.")
print("Tests: all within 1-2C WHEN AMOUNT IS RIGHT. Amount > pattern.")

t: What a Spreader Card Is and When to Use One
title: What a Spreader Card Is and When to Use One
description: A spreader card is a small flat plastic blade — often included with paste tubes — used to manually spread compound into a thin even layer across the heatspreader. Use it when you want verified full coverage (show builds, high-TDP CPUs) or with thick pastes that do not spread well under pressure. The card gives visual proof of coverage before the cooler goes on.

demo.program:
print("Spreader card: flat blade, spreads paste manually to thin even layer.")
print("Use for: verified full coverage, thick pastes, high-TDP CPUs, show builds.")
print("Payoff: visual proof of coverage BEFORE the cooler mounts.")

t: How Much Paste: The Right Amount by CPU Size
title: How Much Paste: The Right Amount by CPU Size
description: Mainstream CPUs (like AM5/LGA1700 size): a pea about 4-5 mm — roughly 0.1 g. Large HEDT/threadripper dies: a line or five-dot pattern, more like 0.2-0.3 g. Too much squeezes out the sides (messy but harmless with non-conductive paste); too little leaves hot corners. When in doubt, slightly more beats slightly less — excess squeezes out, shortage does not fix itself.

demo.program:
print("Mainstream (AM5/LGA1700): pea 4-5mm (~0.1g).")
print("HEDT/threadripper: line or 5-dot (~0.2-0.3g).")
print("Too much: squeezes out (harmless, non-conductive). Too little: hot corners.")
print("Doubt? slightly MORE: excess squeezes out, shortage doesn't fix itself.")

t: Spreader Card Technique: The Thin Even Coat
title: Spreader Card Technique: The Thin Even Coat
description: The technique: pea of paste center, card held at ~45 degrees, smooth strokes from center outward, one thin pass — then STOP. The layer should be thin enough to see the heatspreader faintly through it. Multiple passes and overworking trap air bubbles. One confident pass beats five fussy ones; the cooler's pressure finishes the job.

demo.program:
print("45-degree card, center-outward, ONE thin pass, then STOP.")
print("Thin enough to faintly see heatspreader through it.")
print("Overworking traps air. One confident pass > five fussy ones.")

t: Paste Types: Ceramic, Carbon, Metal, and Liquid Metal
title: Paste Types: Ceramic, Carbon, Metal, and Liquid Metal
description: Ceramic/silicone pastes (like Arctic MX-4): safe, non-conductive, the default — 5-8 W/mK. Carbon-based: slightly better, still safe. Metal-based: better still but capacitive — keep off components. Liquid metal (gallium): 70+ W/mK, conductive, corrodes aluminum — expert only, never with aluminum coolers. For 95% of builders, a good ceramic paste is the right answer.

demo.program:
print("Ceramic (MX-4 style): safe, non-conductive, 5-8 W/mK. THE default.")
print("Carbon: slightly better, safe. Metal-based: capacitive, keep off parts.")
print("Liquid metal: 73 W/mK, CONDUCTIVE, eats aluminum. EXPERT ONLY.")
print("95% of builders: good ceramic paste. Done.")

t: Use Case: Mainstream CPU Paste Job
title: Use Case: Mainstream CPU Paste Job
description: The standard job: clean both surfaces to shine, pea of ceramic paste center of the heatspreader (or card-spread for proof), mount cooler straight down without sliding, tighten in a cross pattern gradually. Boot and check temps at idle and load — a good mount shows even core temps. Sliding the cooler during mounting is the classic mistake: it smears the layer into unevenness.

demo.program:
steps = ["clean to shine (both)", "pea center (or card-spread)",
         "cooler STRAIGHT down (no slide)", "cross-pattern tighten, gradual",
         "boot: check idle + load temps, even cores = good mount"]
for i, s in enumerate(steps, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {s}")
print("Sliding the cooler = smearing the layer = the classic mistake.")

t: Use Case: GPU Die Paste (Delidded-Style Care)
title: Use Case: GPU Die Paste (Delidded-Style Care)
description: GPU dies are bare silicon — no heatspreader — so paste goes directly on the fragile die. Use a card-spread for guaranteed edge-to-edge coverage (bare dies punish the pea method's uncertainty), keep paste off the surrounding SMD components, and mount with even pressure. Non-conductive paste only — a squeeze-out onto SMDs with conductive paste kills cards.

demo.program:
print("Bare die: card-spread for edge-to-edge certainty (pea is uncertain here).")
print("Keep paste OFF surrounding SMDs. Even mounting pressure.")
print("NON-CONDUCTIVE paste only: conductive squeeze-out on SMDs kills cards.")

title: The Cross-Pattern Mounting Sequence
description: Cooler screws tighten in a cross (X) pattern, a half-turn at a time, cycling until snug — this seats the cooler flat instead of rocking onto one corner. Rocking traps a thick paste wedge on one side and starves the other. Final torque: snug, not crushed; over-tightening bows boards. The pattern matters as much as the paste.

demo.program:
print("Cross (X) pattern, half-turn cycles, until snug.")
print("Seats flat: rocking traps thick wedge one side, starves other.")
print("Snug not crushed (bows boards). Pattern matters as much as paste.")

t: How Often to Repaste: The Honest Schedule
title: How Often to Repaste: The Honest Schedule
description: Quality paste lasts 3-5 years before drying meaningfully; cheap paste can dry in 1-2. Repaste when load temps creep up 5-10°C from the baseline with clean fans and heatsinks — the temp log proves it. Do not repaste on a schedule for fun: every repaste risks the mount, and good paste outlives most upgrade cycles. Data, not calendar, decides.

demo.program:
print("Quality paste: 3-5 years. Cheap: 1-2.")
print("Repaste signal: load temps +5-10C over baseline (fans/heatsinks clean).")
print("Temp log decides, not the calendar. Good paste outlives upgrade cycles.")

t: Spreader Card vs Pea vs X-Pattern: Test Results
title: Spreader Card vs Pea vs X-Pattern: Test Results
description: Controlled tests consistently show 1-3°C between methods with correct amounts — the spreader's advantage is coverage certainty, not magic degrees. Where spread wins measurably: large dies, thick pastes, and beginners (visual feedback). Where pea wins: speed and simplicity. The honest summary: pick the method you execute well; execution beats method.

demo.program:
print("Tests: 1-3C between methods (correct amounts).")
print("Spread wins: large dies, thick pastes, beginners (visual feedback).")
print("Pea wins: speed, simplicity.")
print("Honest: the method you execute well beats the 'best' method done badly.")

t: Cleaning Up: Paste Where It Should Not Be
title: Cleaning Up: Paste Where It Should Not Be
description: Squeeze-out on the board: IPA and lint-free, one-direction wipes, patience — non-conductive paste is messy but harmless. Paste in the socket: the nightmare — do NOT use IPA floods (it spreads); pick out carefully with tweezers and a dry brush, and accept that socket paste can mean board replacement. Prevention (right amount, no slide) beats every cleanup.

demo.program:
print("On board (non-conductive): IPA + lint-free, one direction, patience. Harmless.")
print("IN SOCKET: nightmare. No IPA floods (spreads it). Tweezers + dry brush.")
print("Socket paste can = board replacement. Prevention beats cleanup, always.")

t: Buying Guide: Paste and Spreader Value
title: Buying Guide: Paste and Spreader Value
description: A 4 g tube of quality ceramic paste (MX-4/MX-6 class) costs 8-12 dollars and does 10-20 applications — paste is the cheapest performance in PC building. Spreader cards often come free with the tube; standalone applicator kits add little. Skip exotic pastes until you have maxed the basics: a perfect mount with MX-4 beats a sloppy mount with liquid metal.

demo.program:
print("4g quality ceramic: $8-12 = 10-20 applications. Cheapest performance in PCs.")
print("Cards often free with tube; applicator kits add little.")
print("Perfect mount + MX-4 BEATS sloppy mount + liquid metal. Basics first.")

t: Advanced: Lapping and the Pursuit of Flat
title: Advanced: Lapping and the Pursuit of Flat
description: Lapping — sanding the heatspreader/cooler base flatter with progressively finer grit — can gain 2-5°C on badly concave surfaces, at the cost of warranty and hours. Modern coolers are flat enough that lapping rarely pays. The spreader card actually diagnoses concavity: paste pooling in the center means a concave surface worth addressing (or replacing).

demo.program:
print("Lapping: sands surfaces flatter, 2-5C on bad concavity, kills warranty, hours.")
print("Modern coolers: flat enough, rarely pays.")
print("Card diagnoses: paste pooling center = concave (address or replace).")
